description: I seek members who are interested in the challenge and have relevant skills (for example, coding, data analysis, statistics).
summary:
Mars once had lakes that dried up and left salts behind. On Earth, the Aral Sea in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan has done the same thing within one lifetime, and satellites recorded every year of it. We built a process analog for drying Martian lakes from open NASA and partner data, then tested it on Mars.

First, we dated when each 30 m pixel of the Aral seabed dried, from 1985 to 2021 (35,000 km²). We matched about 11 million NASA EMIT mineral pixels to those dates. Carbonate and clay are most common on the oldest ground, gypsum peaks in the middle, and salt-type labels dominate the youngest ground. Clays fall with drying date in 12 of 12 scenes and the salt-type label rises in 11 of 11, and Landsat shows a matching trend across the whole basin.

Then we turned this into a rule that can be tested: "salts end up in the last 23% of a basin to dry." We checked it against 642 Martian chloride deposits using NASA MOLA elevation data. Martian salts do collect in closed lows (60% vs 38% of nearby ground), but not in the last-to-dry part (20% vs 23% by chance). So most Martian salts probably came from small ponds, not one big drying lake.

Finally, a global search over every dry-climate basin from 52°S to 52°N ranks the Aral first among lakes that dried in the satellite era, 17 times ahead of the next region. A second test shows why the Aral is special: it left 13,400 km² of ground that never flooded again, 37 times more than any other drying lake we checked.
details:
What it does

The challenge allows analogs for Moon-base locations or Mars landing sites; we chose Mars, because a salt lake drying by evaporation is a Mars process with no counterpart on the Moon. The project makes the dried Aral seabed (the Aralkum) a dated, measured analog for evaporating Martian lake basins, tests what it predicts on Mars, and turns the method into a global search for similar sites on Earth. It has five parts:

  1. A drying-year map. For every 30 m pixel of the Aral basin, the year the permanent lake left, from 1985 to 2021, plus how often the pixel flooded again. It is a public Earth Engine app anyone can explore.
  2. Minerals against drying date. NASA EMIT mineral maps (12 scenes, about 11 million pixels) and Landsat 8/9 over three summers, both compared with the drying date.
  3. A Mars test. A rule taken from the Aral, tested on 642 mapped Martian chloride deposits with NASA MOLA elevation data, plus a close look at the proposed Terra Sirenum lake basin.
  4. A global search. Every river basin on Earth between 52°S and 52°N, ranked by how much permanent lake water became land since 1984, keeping only those in dry climates.
  5. A field route and a dust-source map. A 90 km route with four stops on ground of known age, from salt crust to clay and carbonate, for testing instruments. The same map separates the two kinds of dust-source ground that field studies describe.

How it works

  • Dating the seabed: JRC Global Surface Water (built from Landsat) gives each pixel's water status every year from 1984 to 2021. Drying year = last year of permanent water + 1. The basin outline from elevation alone is 68,206 km², close to the documented pre-1960 sea area of about 68,000 km². Our 2021 water area (7,793 km²) is close to the roughly 8,000 km² reported.
    • Clays fall with later drying in 12 of 12 scenes.
    • Carbonates fall in 9 of 9 on ground that never flooded again.
    • Gypsum peaks in a middle period in 6 of 7 scenes.
    • A salt-type label rises in 11 of 11. NASA has not validated this label, and we say so.
  • Second instrument: the Landsat 8/9 SWIR1/SWIR2 ratio rises with drying year across the whole basin (rank correlation +0.73 to +0.81 in 2022, 2023 and 2024). Two zones break the pattern, and documented flood pulses explain them (Amu Darya 2010; North Aral outflow 2017).
  • Mars: we filled every closed low on Mars between 70°S and 20°N in MOLA topography. For each chloride deposit inside a low, we computed how much of that low would already be dry when the water left the deposit. We fixed the threshold (77.4%) from Aral data before looking at Mars, and checked the code on random points: it gives 23%, as expected by chance.
  • Global search: JRC Global Surface Water transitions (1984 vs 2021), HydroBASINS river basins and a TerraClimate dryness index. Neighbouring basins are joined into lake regions and ranked.

Results

  • Earth: surface minerals on the Aral seabed change with drying date in the order evaporation predicts: least soluble first (carbonate), then gypsum, then the most soluble salts. Two instruments agree.
  • Mars: chloride deposits sit in closed lows far more often than the ground around them (60% vs 38%, z = 12; it holds in 214 of 333 two-degree cells). Inside those lows they are not in the last-to-dry band (20% vs 22.6% by chance, p = 0.88). Most Martian chlorides therefore do not look like the end product of one large drying lake. This matches Leask & Ehlmann (2022), who describe them as small, shallow ponds.
  • Terra Sirenum: in MOLA, the closed low under the proposed lake's salt flats has a rim at 1,276 m and is 254 m deep, matching the published 1,280 m contour and "at least 200 m" depth. But it covers only about 3,600 km², a tenth of the published 30,000 km².
  • Ground truth from published field work: two of our three mineral trends agree with field studies: carbonate falls and salts rise from old to young ground. Clay disagrees: field work finds more clay towards the new seabed. That points to thin salt crusts hiding clay from orbit, a pitfall that matters on Mars too.
  • Field route: four stops on ground that never flooded again: salts (dried 2015–21), gypsum and clay (2005–14), clay (1995–2004), clay with carbonate (1985–94). Coordinates are in the repository.
  • Global search: the Aral comes first (33,400 km² of permanent water became land, within 5% of our own map). Next come Great Salt Lake, the north-western Great Basin lakes, Lake Poopó, the Sistan Hamun lakes (hyper-arid, 89% dried) and Lake Urmia. Three of the top eleven regions are in Kazakhstan.
  • Only the Aral leaves a large surface of known age: 13,400 km² of seabed never flooded again after the water left (38%). That is 37 times more than the next lake (Sistan) and 11 times more than ten other drying lakes combined. Most drying lakes, such as Lake Urmia (99% flooded again), are seasonal salt flats whose surfaces cannot be dated.

What is analogous, how much, and what is not

Dimension

Match

Evidence

Process: a closed salt lake drying by evaporation

Strong

The Aral grew saltier as it shrank. Minerals change with drying date in the evaporation order (12 EMIT scenes, Landsat).

Scale

Good

Aral basin 68,000 km². Proposed Terra Sirenum lake: 30,000 km² or more.

Wet-dry cycling

Good

60% of the new seabed flooded again in a later year. Gale crater shows repeated wetting and drying.

Where salts end up inside a basin

Weak for most of Mars

Tested on 642 Martian deposits: not in the last-to-dry part.

Mineral mix

Partial

Martian chlorides rarely come with carbonates and sulfates; the Aral has all three.

Dust

Qualitative

The Aralkum is a major source of salty dust, and Martian dust also carries salts. We did not measure this.

Temperature, air pressure, gravity, radiation, life

Poor

Earth cannot reproduce these. The Aral seabed also has plants, rain and farm chemicals.

Zhamanshin crater: an impact site in Kazakhstan relevant to the Moon and Mars

This young impact structure is an impact-geology training site; Artemis astronauts will need to read impact rocks. We tested whether free 30 m elevation data can see its newly proposed 26.5 km multi-ring size. They cannot: there is no clear ring at 13.25 km radius. Subtle impact structures can be missed at this resolution, which also matters for site selection on the Moon and Mars.

How it helps exploration

  • A ready field route. Four stops with coordinates let instrument or rover teams test against an evaporite sequence of known age.
  • Salty dust. The map separates the erodible old rim from young salt crust, the two dust-source grounds described in field studies. That is useful for dust modelling and seabed planting on Earth, and for testing salty-dust instruments for Mars.
  • Testing orbital instruments. EMIT is an imaging spectrometer like CRISM at Mars. The Aral lets us check how such instruments see an evaporite basin of known age. It also shows two pitfalls: salt crusts can hide clays, and automatic labels can mislead.
  • Choosing where to land and sample. If a Martian basin held one big lake, look for carbonates on the oldest, highest ground and the most soluble salts in the last-to-dry lows.
  • A quick test from elevation alone. It checks whether a Martian salt deposit fits the big-lake picture, and runs on all mapped deposits in seconds.
  • A ranked list of new Earth candidates. The global search lists other places to study this process, and the drying-date check says which of them can be dated.

Limits

  • Everything is from orbit, with no ground samples.
  • Some EMIT mineral labels are not validated, and EMIT cannot see halite.
  • The scenes are from one year.
  • Today's Mars is shaped by billions of years of later craters and erosion.
  • MOLA at 3.7 km resolution misses small lows.
  • The global search compares only 1984 and 2021, and its lake names were assigned from coordinates.
  • Full list in the README.

Tools

Google Earth Engine (JavaScript); Python (numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-image, matplotlib); NASA AppEEARS; NASA PDS. All code, tables and charts are in the GitHub repository and can be rerun.
